Nagaland

See01 The state

Nagaland at a glance

Most people in Nagaland can read and write. The next question is how many stay in school.

Compare literacy with the five most literate states

Nagaland is shown at its actual figure. The axis begins at 70%, which makes differences look larger than they are.

Terms used on this page
Right-age enrolmentChildren of the official age who are in school, per 100 of that age.
All-ages enrolmentEveryone in a stage, any age, per 100 of the official age.
TransitionOf those finishing a stage, how many enter the next one.
DropoutStudents who leave school in a year, as a share of those enrolled.
Details and source

Census of India 2011 (literacy, age 7+), the last full census, so it is 15 years old. UDISE+ 2025–26 (net enrolment rate: students of the official age group enrolled at a stage, divided by that age group's population; dropout: annual rate, Classes 9–10). State literacy figures: Census of India 2011 final totals (Registrar General), rounded; verify against the Census primary abstract before citing.

Literacy is high. Does schooling keep pace with it?

See02 Who is studying

338,677 students
across four stages.

This is everyone enrolled today, shown by stage. The size of a stage does not tell us who has left.

Details and source

These totals do not show who is missing. District figures come next.

See03 Districts

Eleven districts show very different levels of enrolment.

Dimapur

Eleven districts on the map schools 2023–24 · enrolment 2024–25

Colour shows enrolment and circle size shows government schools. Choose a stage to compare.

Details and source

Census 2011 literacy, age 7+, on 2011 district boundaries. Nagaland Economic Survey 2025–26, Annex 4.4: net enrolment rate 2024–25. Rates above 100% can include students from outside the district or reflect population estimates; they do not mean every local child is enrolled. On the map, districts are shaded in four steps, from the lowest quarter to the highest quarter of districts for the chosen measure.

The gap is widest at higher secondary, so the step up from Class 10 deserves a closer look.

See04 Where progression slows

Fewer students continue into Class 11 than at any earlier step.

continued from 10th to 11th in Nagaland

Dropout and transition measure different things, so they should not be added together.

Details and source

Dropout counts students who leave in Classes 9–10 in a year. Transition counts students who enter Class 11 the next year. UDISE+. Transition rate: students entering the first class of the next stage compared with enrolment in the last class of the previous stage the year before. Each house is a separate group in that year, not one cohort followed through school. Each figure is 1 student in 100, rounded. Transfers recorded by the source count as continuing.

The evidence behind it: exam results, what happens next, dropout

Step 1 of 3

Before Class 11

Do students pass the Class 10 exam?

In 2026, 43% of government-school candidates passed, against 86% in private schools. The records do not show how many who fail re-sit or leave.

Details and source

Nagaland Board of School Education results archive. Class 10 (HSLC) pass rate, percent of candidates, by school management. Candidates are not the same group as enrolled students. The records here do not show why rates differ.

After Class 10

What do schools say students do next?

Details and source

Share of reporting schools where more than half of students did this right after Class 10. These are school estimates, not a student count, and the bars cannot be added. NCERT PARAKH Nagaland report.

In Classes 9 and 10

How many students leave school?

Details and source

UDISE+ secondary dropout rate (Classes 9–10), annual. A transfer or study elsewhere counts as continued education, not dropout. A separate state publication reports a different 2024–25 series, so the two are not combined.

What sits alongside the drop? The records mention distance and money.

Act05 What makes it hard

Two factors stand out in the records: how far schools are, and money.

Distance villages assessed · March 2025

Details and source

Nagaland Samagra Shiksha Project Approval Board, March 2025. Villages assessed at each stage against a prescribed distance. Exact local distance cutoffs are unavailable in the evidence used. The data do not show how many students moved.

31% named money survey of 871 leavers · 2018 · most left in middle school

A group of 100 former students, arranged by the reason each gave. Select a reason to see who it covers.

Details and source

NEDFi Nagaland skills survey, 2018. 871 former students, shown per 100 respondents. Most left during middle school. The summary does not link each reason to a stage or outcome, and does not isolate students leaving after 10th.

What happened to those who left: 83% of surveyed school leavers were unemployed at interview survey of 871 leavers · 2018 · most left in middle school

Details and source

NEDFi Nagaland skills survey, 2018. 871 former students; time since leaving school was not reported. The other 6% is unspecified and is not wage work.

More: schools by category

Government schools only, in the 11 districts that report. Bar length is the number of schools.

Details and source

Nagaland Statistical Handbook 2025, table 19.12: government schools by category, 2023–24, 11 reporting districts. Private schools are not included. Longleng lists one government higher-secondary school and Kiphire two.

And for those who carry on, where do they go?

Act06 Where students go next

Details and source

Most Class 12 students plan to study further

In one survey, about 80 in 100 said higher education. The records do not show how many actually went on.

What 2,453 Class 12 students said they plan to do survey · year not confirmed

How many actually went on?Not in the records
Details and source

YouthNet LaunchPad online survey of Class 12 students in 44 government schools; 2,453 listed answers on next step. The survey year is not confirmed in the sources reviewed. These are plans, not outcomes. “Work” adds “get a job” and “other jobs”; the last group adds gap year and vocational training. Shown per 100 answers, rounded.

What we can see insteadAbout 19 in 100 young people aged 18–23 are in higher education AISHE · 2024–25

Take care: the survey counts Class 12 students and their plans, while this counts all young people aged 18–23. The two numbers measure different things, so do not subtract one from the other.

Details and source

Nagaland Department of Higher Education, Annual Administrative Report 2025–26, citing AISHE. Gross enrolment ratio for ages 18–23: 17.3 (2020–21), 18.8, 18.8, 19.66 (2023–24), 19.07 (2024–25). Women 21.7, men 16.5. Total higher-education enrolment 48,439. The report gives no count of students studying outside Nagaland.

What help exists for those who stop?

Act07 What support exists

Some help is in place. This is what the records show.

Class 12th re-examination, 2023. One dot is one candidate.

Details and source

Nagaland DIPR and NBSE, 2023 Class 12th compartmental examination. Reasons for not qualifying or not sitting are unavailable.

414 of 723 out-of-school children mainstreamed

Details and source

Nagaland Samagra Shiksha PAB, March 2025. Children identified in 2019–20; mainstreamed in 2020–21. The later status of the other 309 is not stated. These are programme counts, not long-term attendance.

Taken together, the three drops and the gap show where help is needed first.

Fill the gaps08 Putting it together

Help first where the numbers narrow.

Fewer children are enrolled at every step. After Class 12, no record follows them.
